4:T4e1,UltraX uses function-calling refinement instead of end-to-end text regeneration. The lightweight refiner emits edit operations, not the full rewritten document. Its operation space includes deletion, modification, and insertion, addressing the incomplete edit spaces in earlier function-calling refiners such as ProX and RefineX. Supervision is built through a multi-stage pipeline. Dataset-adaptive prompt optimization first guides an expert LLM to produce higher-quality refined texts. Line Alignment Mapping then converts original-refined text pairs into executable program supervision. Dynamic Context Replacement handles context changes caused by local edits and reduces interference between consecutive operations. Low-confidence examples are filtered, and ratio-controlled sampling balances different operation combinations. At inference time, UltraX uses sliding-window prediction for long documents, global operation aggregation to merge window-level outputs, and post-processing to normalize, validate, and execute the predicted programs. Compared with full-text rewriting, the programmatic route reduces output tokens and makes chunk recombination easier to control. Compared with static rules, it supports instance-level semantic repair.5:T4aa,The provided full-text excerpt states that the evaluation includes from-scratch pretraining of 1B-parameter MiniCPM models, which is the right evidence path for a pretraining-data method. (1) Architecture: each MLP layer in a dense Transformer is augmented with several smaller auxiliary MLP modules, each dedicated to one target capability domain, while the main MLP handles general core capabilities. (2) Training routing: forward and backward passes for auxiliary modules are selectively enabled based on the domain of the current batch. Core data updates only the backbone; data from a specific auxiliary domain updates both the backbone and the corresponding auxiliary module; gradients never flow to unrelated auxiliary modules. This design maps data domains to parameter subspaces, physically isolating the learning of different capabilities. (3) Inference control: ablating an auxiliary module at inference time removes its corresponding capability without retraining; enabling arbitrary subsets of modules produces arbitrary capability profiles from a single deployed model. GRAM combines domain-specific modules, data-dependent selective gradient updates, and per-subset optimizers into an end-to-end pretraining recipe for access control.a:T46f,Experiments span synthetic and realistic dual-use datasets, scale from 50M to 5B parameters, and compare against data filtering (gold standard), model branching, FT-LoRA, and post-hoc unlearning. (1) On the Simple Stories synthetic dataset, GRAM closely matches data filtering on both capability retention and removal. (2) In the 800M-parameter realistic setting, the core corpus is web text + code + arXiv papers, with four auxiliary domains: virology, cybersecurity, nuclear physics, and Lisp code. GRAM matches the all-data baseline on core tasks; matches data filtering and FT-LoRA on auxiliary retention and removal; resists malicious finetuning on removed domains substantially better than post-hoc unlearning, approaching the robustness of data filtering. Enabling multiple auxiliary modules does not cause mutual interference. (3) Under partially labeled data, GRAM achieves far better capability removal than both data filtering and branched finetuning. (4) Across 50M–5B compute-optimal models, GRAM's capability profiles closely track data filtering, and suppression of the target forget capability strengthens with scale.b:T90b,方法很干净。作者从浮点数表示出发，写出在 mantissa 位数为 m 时，参数 wi 的表示间隔 ULP_m(wi)=2^{floor(log2|wi|)-m}。若一次梯度下降更新满足 |Δwi| < 1/2 ULP_m(wi)，按 round-to-nearest 后该坐标保持不变，于是该坐标被冻结。基于这个逐坐标条件，作者定义 frozen fraction f，即一次 step 后 bitwise 不变的参数比例，并把 f 首次达到 1/2 的时刻定义为 freeze time τ*。

更关键的是，他们把条件改写成无量纲形式 ρ_i < 2^{-φ_i}，其中 φ_i 是 log2|wi| 的小数部分，表示参数位于当前 binade 内的相对位置。若 φ_i 近似均匀分布，则 half-ULP 边界对应一个固定的一比特宽区间，其中位阈值给出 ρ* = 1/sqrt(2) ≈ 0.707，没有拟合参数。这个推导解释了为什么冻结阈值是 O(1) 常数，而不是随模型维度变尖锐的相变。

预测器的构造也很直接：先跑一条 fp64 高精度轨迹 {w_t, g_t}，然后对任意目标精度 m，在每个 step 上计算预测冻结比例 \hat f_t(m)=<1[η|g_{t,i}| < 1/2 ULP_m(w_{t,i})]>。\hat f_t 穿过 1/2 的时刻就是预测的 τ*。这里完全不需要低精度训练数据，因此如果预测成立，就说明冻结主要由算术离散化决定，而不是低精度训练反馈改变了动力学。

实验设计上，作者用了两类实现。其一是真实 bf16 硬件。其二是 mantissa-truncation emulator：所有算术在 fp64 中做，但每步后把权重 round 到 m-bit mantissa 网格。这样可以单独研究 mantissa 精度，而不混入 exponent 范围和 denormal 等因素。作者先在 m=7 上验证 emulator 与真实 bf16 一致，再扫 m∈{5,6,7,8,10,12}。这套设计的优点是把问题拆得很清楚：冻结来自权重存储精度本身，而不是某个硬件实现细节。

从全文看，论文还强调了两个细节。第一，冻结 onset 是 crossover，不会因为参数数目变大而变成无限尖锐的临界点，因为 half-ULP band 的宽度天然就是一比特。第二，在多层网络里，全局 L2 聚合的 ρ 可能失真，因为不同层尺度不同，小 bias 向量还可能长期不冻结；因此真正可靠的是逐坐标或分层统计，而不是单个全局标量。这一点对大模型监控很重要。c:T9b4,实验分四层展开，逻辑很完整。

1. frozen-feature 线性 GD + 真实 bf16 硬件：作者先在最简单可控的设定里直接观测冻结。step 100 时 frozen fraction f=0，step 300 时 f=1.0，之后训练最后 90% 的过程参数都保持冻结。用首次完全冻结点读取阈值，得到 ρ*≈0.72。

2. mantissa emulator 扫精度与学习率：在 m=7 上，emulator 对真实 bf16 的 freeze curve 拟合 RMSE 仅 0.002，说明它是可信替身。进一步扫 m∈{5,6,7,8,10,12}，覆盖 128× 的精度跨度，以及 4× 学习率范围，得到稳定阈值 ρ*=0.71，跨设置 coefficient of variation 为 0.06。这里最关键的结果不是单点数值，而是阈值几乎不随精度和学习率变化，只是 freeze time 在大范围移动。

3. 先验预测 τ*：这是全文最有说服力的实验。作者只用高精度轨迹和目标 mantissa 位数预测冻结时间，预测与实测在 384× 的 freeze-time 范围内一致，覆盖从 11 到 4222 steps。对可训练网络的 55 个 clean cells，predicted/measured 的中位比值为 1.00，约 94.5% 的 cell 落在 15% 误差内。更重要的是，预测能跟住个体轨迹差异；某些 run 比邻近设置早两个数量级冻结，预测也能提前指出。

4. 可训练非凸网络与真实数据：
- 两层 tanh teacher-student 回归中，emulator 与真实 bf16 的 freeze curve RMSE 为 0.007，阈值约 ρ*≈0.74；跨 seed 的 within-cell CV 中位数为 0.21。说明冻结并不依赖 frozen features 或凸性。
- 一个约 1e5 参数的 CNN，在 MNIST 上做交叉熵训练。emulator 扫 m∈{5,6,7,8,10}、3 个 seeds，共 15 个 precision-seed cells。这里先验预测达到“逐 cell 完全命中”：预测 freeze step 与实测完全相同，中位比值 1.000，最大误差 0%。真实 bf16 硬件上，m=7 的 freeze curve 也被 emulator 以 RMSE 0.02 复现。

5. 124M GPT-2：摘要里已经给出一个关键信号：在 124M GPT-2 上，如果每步后都把权重约束到 8-bit floating-point grid，训练也会在中途进入冻结区。虽然给出的正文片段没有完整展开 GPT-2 数字，但论文的意图很明确：silent freeze 不是小模型玩具现象，而是会出现在标准 Transformer 训练里。

整体上，最值得记住的数字有三个：阈值 ρ* 大致稳定在 0.71–0.74；高精度轨迹预测 freeze time 的中位比值 1.00；预测覆盖 11 到 4222 steps 的 384× 时间尺度。d:T805,The analysis starts from floating-point spacing. For a format with m mantissa bits, the spacing at coordinate wi is ULP_m(wi)=2^{floor(log2|wi|)-m}. Under round-to-nearest, a gradient step leaves wi unchanged whenever |Δwi| < 1/2 ULP_m(wi). This gives a per-coordinate freeze condition and leads to a measurable frozen fraction f, defined as the proportion of coordinates that remain bitwise unchanged after a step. The freeze time τ* is the first step where f reaches 1/2.

The key theoretical move is to rewrite the condition in dimensionless form as ρ_i < 2^{-φ_i}, where φ_i is the fractional part of log2|wi| and indicates where the weight lies within its binade. If φ_i is approximately equidistributed, the half-ULP boundary occupies a one-bit-wide band, whose median yields a parameter-free threshold ρ*=1/sqrt(2). This explains why the onset is an O(1) crossover rather than a sharp size-dependent phase transition.

The predictor is deliberately simple. Run one fp64 trajectory {w_t, g_t}. For any target mantissa length m, compute the predicted frozen fraction at each step as \hat f_t(m)=<1[η|g_{t,i}| < 1/2 ULP_m(w_{t,i})]>. The predicted τ* is where \hat f_t crosses 1/2. Since the predictor uses no low-precision data, successful prediction would imply that the phenomenon is governed primarily by arithmetic discretization rather than by altered low-precision dynamics.

The experimental design separates arithmetic effects cleanly. Real bf16 hardware establishes that the freeze is physically present. A mantissa-truncation emulator performs all arithmetic in fp64 but rounds weights to an m-bit grid after each step, allowing controlled sweeps over mantissa precision without confounding exponent range or denormals. The paper also emphasizes an important practical nuance: in multilayer networks, a single pooled L2-based ρ can become misleading because layers live at different scales and tiny bias vectors may never freeze. Layerwise or coordinatewise statistics are therefore more informative than a single global scalar.e:T91d,The empirical story is built in stages.

First, in frozen-feature linear gradient descent on real bf16 hardware, the frozen fraction is 0 at step 100 and 1.0 by step 300, after which the iterate remains frozen for the final 90% of training. Reading the threshold at the first fully frozen point gives ρ*≈0.72.

Second, the mantissa-truncation emulator is validated against real bf16 at m=7, reproducing the freeze curve with RMSE 0.002. Sweeping m in {5,6,7,8,10,12} spans a 128x precision range, and varying the learning rate spans another 4x. Across this grid, the threshold remains stable at ρ*=0.71 with coefficient of variation 0.06. The main point is that precision and learning rate shift the freeze time substantially, but not the threshold itself.

Third, the a-priori prediction of freeze time is the strongest result in the paper. Using only the high-precision trajectory and the target mantissa length, predicted and measured τ* agree across a 384x range of freeze times, from 11 to 4222 steps. On 55 clean trainable-network cells, the median predicted/measured ratio is 1.00, and about 94.5% of cells fall within 15%. The predictor also tracks trajectory-specific outliers rather than only average trends.

Fourth, the phenomenon survives beyond convex toy settings. In a two-layer trainable tanh teacher-student regression problem, the emulator matches real bf16 with RMSE 0.007 and the threshold is around ρ*≈0.74. In a CNN with about 1e5 parameters trained on MNIST with cross-entropy, the emulator sweep over m in {5,6,7,8,10} and 3 seeds yields exact freeze-step prediction in all 15 precision-seed cells: median ratio 1.000 and maximum error 0%. On real bf16 hardware at m=7, the emulator still matches the freeze curve with RMSE 0.02.

Finally, the paper extends the observation to a 124M GPT-2 transformer with weights constrained to an 8-bit floating-point grid after each step. The full numerical details are not included in the excerpt here, but the inclusion of this experiment is important: the authors are not claiming a toy-only effect. They are arguing that the same arithmetic mechanism appears in standard Transformer training as well.

The numbers worth retaining are the threshold range 0.71–0.74, the median prediction ratio of 1.00, and the 384x span of accurately predicted freeze times.f:T793,Read it in three passes: definition, predictor, generalization.

Start with the opening part of Results where the paper derives the half-ULP condition and rewrites it in terms of ρ and φ. That section determines whether the work is merely empirical or whether it truly pins the effect on floating-point arithmetic. Then inspect Figure 1 carefully: the real-bf16 versus emulator freeze curves, and the predicted-versus-measured freeze times. If those plots are convincing, the main claim is already in good shape.

Next, go to the Methods section for the derivation of ρ*=1/sqrt(2). The important question is not the algebra itself, but why a parameter-free threshold emerges and how credible the equidistributed-φ assumption is in practice. This is also where one should think about whether different parameter classes in large models, such as embeddings, norms, and biases, might violate the assumption.

Then read the trainable tanh and CNN sections. They answer the obvious objection that the effect might only hold in linear or frozen-feature settings. The CNN discussion is especially useful because it shows why a single pooled ρ can fail in multilayer models with heterogeneous scales. That point is highly relevant for real LLM monitoring.

If time is limited, at least read the GPT-2 setup and the main figure around it. The practical questions to keep in mind are: how weights are projected to the low-precision grid, whether AdamW plus cosine is still used, and at what stage of training the freeze appears. Natural follow-up questions are whether fp32 master weights largely remove the issue, whether Adam moments merely delay rather than eliminate freezing, and whether cooldown, weight decay, or norm control can keep ρ away from the danger zone.

A full careful read is about 45 to 60 minutes. A fast read focused on the main claim can be done in about 20 minutes via Results, Figure 1, and the Transformer experiment.10:T503,Index-1.9B is a Llama-style decoder-only Transformer with RoPE, SwiGLU, and RMSNorm. The authors choose a relatively deep 36-layer configuration after a depth-versus-width study at fixed parameter count. The base model has 1.9B non-embedding parameters and is trained on 2.8T tokens, with a Chinese-to-English ratio of about 4:5, 6% code, and roughly 10% curated books, encyclopedias, papers, and STEM material. A Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule is used, and the curated subset is upweighted during the decay phase. Data cleaning relies mainly on heuristic rules; classifiers are used conservatively for hard cases, with labels bootstrapped from a larger Index-Large model. Deduplication combines Spark-based global MinHash with exact substring duplicate detection based on suffix-array tooling, allowing repeated spans at arbitrary positions inside documents to be found. The tokenizer is a compact 65,029-token SentencePiece BPE tokenizer. Chinese vocabulary is trained separately with a shorter maximum piece length, the vocabulary is kept small to reduce embedding overhead, and the usual Llama-style prepended whitespace is removed. The report also identifies unusually large LM-head gradients and rare-token oscillation as stability issues, then compares stabilization mechanisms.11:T4ae,M+Adam combines two update branches:
- Additive branch: Adam/AdamW-style moment estimates and an additive step in weight space. This is crucial near zero and for sign flips, but in low precision it can stall at large magnitudes because updates smaller than the local quantization bin are rounded away.
- Multiplicative branch: Madam-style relative (scale) updates so the effective step scales with |w|, helping the optimizer move on coarse grids at large magnitudes. But multiplicative updates preserve sign and cannot escape exact zeros.

A notable detail is the derivation of the multiplicative branch via exponent-space gradients: using floating-point decomposition w = m·2^e, the method expresses the gradient w.r.t. the exponent in a form that does not require explicitly tracking e, then applies second-moment normalization. Practical safeguards include a threshold τ to avoid division by tiny weights and clipping of relative factors.

The combination is designed so multiplicative updates dominate where quantization bins are large, while additive updates handle the near-zero and sign-change regime. The paper also provides a monotone descent proof under standard smoothness assumptions.12:T450,The analysis starts with a separable strongly convex quadratic and an affine-variance noise model, where the gradient-noise variance has an additive term σ0² and a multiplicative term σ1²||∇f||². When σ0=0, the noise is a scale family and vanishes at the optimum. For SGD in one coordinate, the second moment follows an exactly multiplicative recursion with contraction r(η)=(1-ηλ)²+η²σ1²λ². The optimal fixed learning rate is η*=1/(λ(1+σ1²)), giving contraction σ1²/(1+σ1²), and the best WSD cooldown fraction is zero. For signSGD and normalized methods under the same multiplicative noise, the probability of stepping in the correct direction is independent of the iterate scale. The dynamics reduce to an analyzable lattice walk, producing a final loss floor of Θ(η²). Cooldown helps because it reduces the step granularity. With any additive noise component, σ0>0, every method has an η-dependent floor. The paper then checks robustness under local (L0,L1)-smoothness, multidimensional normalized SGD, momentum, and heavy-tailed noise without relying on finite moments.13:T45d,Agora is built around three constraints absent in centralized training: (1) the model is sharded primarily via pipeline parallelism, using subspace networks to compress cross-stage activations by roughly two orders of magnitude so that PP is viable over internet-grade links; (2) data-parallel replicas do not synchronize gradients with a per-step all-reduce; instead, sparse asynchronous parameter averaging exchanges only a small subset of slow-moving weights, infrequently and in the background, so weight synchronization overlaps with computation and never blocks the optimizer step; (3) fault tolerance is built into the training step rather than implemented as an external recovery mechanism, so joins, leaves, and heterogeneity are handled continuously, and newcomers catch up from stale weights without disrupting the run. On top of this, the system adopts ideas from Unextractable Protocol Models (UPM): because the model is model-parallel, no single participant ever holds the full weights, aiming to make weight extraction from individual nodes infeasible. The overall paradigm is termed Protocol Learning.14:T5d4,The contribution is not a new optimizer but a tightly controlled reassessment. The setup has three important pieces. First, the authors choose problem families that can be systematically swept: symmetric PSD factorization, matrix completion, and NMF. These cover unconstrained low-rank recovery, missing-observation settings, and constrained factorization with nonnegativity and redundancy. Second, they run equal-budget, carefully tuned comparisons across Muon, Adam, AdamW, and GD, instead of inheriting community-default hyperparameters. This matters because Muon is sensitive to learning rate, momentum, weight decay, and the approximation details of the orthogonalization step. Third, they interpret results through the lens of what orthogonalization is actually doing. Muon approximately orthogonalizes matrix-shaped gradients, flattening singular-value anisotropy and moving closer to steepest descent under the spectral norm. One might expect that to help on spectral problems, but the paper shows that in classical matrix factorization this does not automatically beat coordinate-wise adaptivity; AdamW’s per-coordinate scaling is often more useful under ill-conditioning. Where Muon does help is NMF: orthogonalized updates appear to discourage factor collapse and reduce redundant directions, leading to more diverse factors. So the gain may come less from faster fitting of dominant singular directions and more from an implicit regularization effect on representation geometry.15:T418,The experimental contribution is about relative behavior across regimes rather than a single headline number. Four findings stand out. First, on standard low-rank matrix factorization, Muon’s advantage mostly vanishes after fair tuning, with AdamW and GD reaching similar or better convergence and final error. Second, on matrix completion, Muon again does not show a stable lead, which weakens the simple intuition that spectral normalization should automatically help on spectrally structured tasks. Third, on NMF, Muon shows a more consistent advantage, especially in overparameterized settings or when factor redundancy is more severe, yielding better reconstruction and less factor overlap. Fourth, ill-conditioning alone does not hand the win to Muon; in many cases AdamW’s adaptive scaling remains stronger. The abstract truncates before detailed numbers, but the full paper’s value is the systematic sweep over conditioning, parameterization, and task variants, with conclusions grounded in tuned comparisons rather than one-off runs.16:T43d,The framework separates three axes of inference-time scaling. Reasoning scaling spends more tokens before producing an answer. Sampling scaling generates more attempts and selects one. Interaction scaling alternates between proposal, external observation, and revision. The paper defines grounded feedback as observations from an instrument that measures the artifact’s actual behavior or form: running tests, rendering a page and measuring element positions, querying an external source, or measuring a layout. It also defines grounded evaluation as using such observations as the score. A coverage principle ties the two together: feedback helps only for defects that the instrument can observe. This explains why a linter may be grounded but ineffective for behavioral bugs, and why a screenshot-reading VLM can fail as a layout judge. The screenshot may crop away overflow, and small overlaps may be below the judge’s effective visual acuity. The contribution is not another agent loop; it is a sharper account of what kind of feedback and metric make interaction scaling real.17:T411,The experiments cover seven artifact-producing modalities: code, web pages, slides, figures, animations, video edits, and research reports. Grounded execution feedback raises two hard coding suites to a 100% pass rate. Grounded geometry feedback removes 40% to 74% of measured layout defects across four visual modalities. A dense academic-figure case shows the evaluation problem clearly: a standard screenshot VLM judge marks 14 of 15 single-shot renders as perfect, while direct measurement finds only 3 clean outputs. Under equal token budgets, reasoning-only and best-of-N saturate; best-of-N saturates even with an oracle verifier, while interaction methods continue improving. The proposer-reviewer harness reaches the gains with lower token cost and zero reported seed variance. Instrument ablations support the grounding thesis: execution feedback beats critique for behavioral bugs, a linter adds little when it observes the wrong property, and a screenshot VLM reviewer worsens slide geometry while a geometry reviewer repairs it.18:T4c8,The method decomposes total GRPO post-training compute into C_search, C_learning, and C_reward. C_search covers autoregressive rollout generation. C_learning covers policy optimization, including an effective update-cost model for LoRA that accounts for trainable adapters as well as the frozen backbone forward and activation costs. C_reward covers reward or verifier inference, which is negligible for rule-based rewards but can be substantial for learned feedback such as process reward models. The main allocation variable is the update fraction ρ = C_learning / C_total. Low ρ corresponds to search- or feedback-heavy runs; high ρ corresponds to update-heavy runs. This differs from common reporting practice because reward-model inference is not treated as free. A PRM-based run and a rule-based run can have the same total FLOPs while buying different amounts of exploration and learning. The empirical setting uses LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5 policies trained with GRPO on mathematical reasoning tasks, and compares model sizes, allocation ratios, reward systems, and evaluation targets. RACE is introduced as a pilot-grid protocol for locating useful allocation regimes before spending budget on larger validation runs.19:T440,The experiments use GRPO post-training of LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5 policies on math reasoning tasks. Four findings are central. First, model size and allocation are coupled under a fixed budget: larger policies cost more per token, so the same budget yields fewer rollouts and fewer updates. As a result, a larger policy is not automatically the best post-training choice. Second, the best observed update fraction changes with model size; no single search-versus-learning split dominates. Third, reward design changes the compute frontier. Rule-based rewards leave most non-update compute for policy rollout, while learned feedback spends part of the budget on reward-model inference. Fourth, evaluation target matters. Native training reward, pass@1 symbolic accuracy, and common-judge process scores can select different allocations. The available text does not expose reproducible numerical tables, exact model-size lists, or absolute gain values, so the safest reading is that the empirical evidence supports conditional allocation frontiers rather than a single winning operating point.1a:Tb27,方法名叫 Hidden Decoding。核心做法是把原始序列中的每个 token 沿 sequence 维度扩展成 n 个 stream，然后在一次标准前向里处理这条更长的序列，但只对最终 stream 施加 next-token loss。这样，中间 stream 提供的是“隐藏计算”，不是额外可见 token。它和 chain-of-thought 或 test-time visible reasoning 的区别在于：额外计算发生在隐状态里，不增加训练目标里的显式文本监督。

这套设计有两个关键点，缺一不可。

第一，per-stream embedding replication。若只是简单复制同一个 token n 次，多个 stream 的初始状态几乎相同，模型很难学出有分工的内部计算。作者为每个 stream 复制一套词嵌入表，把 token x_i 扩成 (E1(x_i), E2(x_i), ..., En(x_i))。continued pretraining 过程中，这些 embedding table 会逐渐分化，让不同 stream 承担不同的表示角色。这个设计很像给“同一个 token 的多步内部思考”提供不同起点，否则 sequence expansion 很容易退化成重复计算。

第二，persistent intermediate KV。此前一些 length-scaling 方案，比如 PHD，为了不让推理成本爆炸，会把中间重复 token 的 KV 设为 transient，只在当前 token 内部起作用，不作为后续位置的上下文保留。这样虽然便宜，但中间计算不能跨位置积累，能力上更像局部 refinement。Hidden Decoding 反过来保留所有 stream 的 KV，让前面位置在中间 stream 上形成的计算结果，能被后面 token 继续访问。作者认为，只有这样，中间 stream 才不只是“当前 token 的额外层数”，而是能形成真正可持续的 latent computation。

问题随之而来：如果对 nL 长序列做全连接注意力，成本会从原来的 O(L^2) 变成 O(n^2 L^2)，在长上下文和大模型上不可接受。为此论文提出 Stream-Factorized Attention。做法是把跨 stream 的信息交换限制在少数层：大多数层只在各自 stream 内做注意力，只有少数“交换层”允许 stream 间通信，而且这些层沿用 base model 原本的注意力模式，比如 sliding-window 或 full attention。这样，绝大多数层避免了对整个 nL 序列做稠密注意力，额外成本更接近对 n 的线性增长，而不是平方增长。

从建模角度看，这个方法和 recurrent-depth Transformer 的差异很明确。looped 模型是在深度维度重复使用同一组 block，计算图有显式回环；Hidden Decoding 则把额外计算摊平到序列维度，仍然保持一次标准前向，因此天然兼容现有的并行训练栈。和普通 token repetition 也不同，它不是把重复 token 当作可见上下文噪声，而是通过独立 embedding、持久 KV 和受控跨 stream 交互，把重复位置变成内部计算槽位。1b:T7e9,实验分两部分，分别验证“能否扩到大规模”和“扩展因子 n 是否形成新的 scaling”。

第一部分是大规模能力验证。作者训练了 WeLM-HD4-80B 和 WeLM-HD4-617B，其中 HD4 表示每个 token 扩成 4 个 stream。对照组分别是同 backbone 的 WeLM-80B 和 WeLM-617B。结果上，80B 版本在九个共享 benchmark 上全部提升，文中点名的增益包括 SciCode 45.8→50.0，PHYBench 69.8→73.8。617B 版本同样在九个共享 benchmark 上全部提升，包括 GPQA Diamond 89.1→91.2，HLE 33.6→35.4，FrontierMath 49.0→51.0。这里一个重要细节是：这些比较使用的是相同的、较早期的 SFT-only post-training recipe，没有引入 RL。这样做的好处是把变量控制得更干净，说明增益主要来自 continued pretraining 阶段的 Hidden Decoding，而不是后续对齐流程差异。

第二部分是 expansion factor 的 scaling 实验。作者在 80B 上做 progressive expansion，把 n 从 2 提到 4 再到 8。结果显示 MMLU 单调提升，85.0→86.7→87.5；Pile-test BPB 从 0.386 降到 0.378。前者说明下游能力随隐藏计算增加而继续增长，后者说明语言建模损失也同步改善，不只是 post-train 指标偶然上涨。对预训练研究者来说，BPB 的下降很关键，因为它表明 Hidden Decoding 不是单纯把推理 benchmark 做高，而是在基础建模质量上也有收益。

从论文叙述看，作者还做了若干设计消融，重点应包括：是否必须保留 intermediate KV、是否必须使用 per-stream embedding、跨 stream 交换层的密度如何影响效果与成本、以及 Stream-Factorized Attention 相比全量跨 stream attention 的效率收益。虽然你给出的全文片段没有完整表格，但这些消融是判断方法是否真的抓住机制的关键。若某个组件去掉后性能明显回落，说明 Hidden Decoding 的有效性不是“把序列拉长”这么简单，而是依赖于可持续的多流内部状态。1c:Ta0f,Hidden Decoding expands each input token into n streams along the sequence dimension, processes the expanded sequence in one standard forward pass, and applies the next-token loss only to the final stream. The intermediate streams act as hidden computation rather than visible reasoning tokens.

Two design choices are central.

First, per-stream embedding replication. If the same token were simply repeated n times with the same embedding table, the streams would start from nearly identical states and the extra computation could collapse into redundant processing. The paper therefore replicates the vocabulary embedding table into n stream-specific tables, so token x_i becomes (E1(x_i), E2(x_i), ..., En(x_i)). During continued pretraining, these tables can diverge and give different streams different representational roles.

Second, persistent intermediate KV states. Some earlier length-scaling approaches keep repeated-token KV transient so that intermediate computation helps only within the current token and does not persist as context for later positions. That keeps inference cheaper, but it limits the extra computation to local refinement. Hidden Decoding instead retains the KV of all streams, allowing latent computation accumulated at earlier positions to remain available to later tokens. This is the paper’s key argument for why sequence expansion can become capability scaling rather than mere local smoothing.

The resulting challenge is attention cost. Full attention over an nL-length sequence would scale as O(n^2 L^2), which is not viable for long contexts and large models. The paper introduces Stream-Factorized Attention to control this. Most layers attend only within each stream, while cross-stream communication is allowed only in a subset of layers. Those exchange layers follow the base model’s original attention pattern, such as sliding-window or full attention. This avoids dense attention over the entire expanded sequence in most layers, making the added cost much closer to linear in n than quadratic.

Relative to recurrent-depth Transformers, the distinction is sharp. Looped models reuse depth and create explicit recurrence through the same blocks, which clashes with pipeline execution. Hidden Decoding flattens extra computation into the sequence dimension and preserves a standard single-pass training graph. Relative to naive token repetition, it adds the ingredients needed to make repeated positions useful as latent compute slots: stream-specific initialization, persistent memory, and controlled cross-stream mixing.1d:T659,The experiments test two claims: scalability to frontier-scale models and capability gains from increasing the expansion factor.

For large-scale validation, the paper trains WeLM-HD4-80B and WeLM-HD4-617B, where HD4 means four streams per token. Each is compared against a matched non-HD backbone. The 80B model improves on all nine shared benchmarks, with reported gains including SciCode 45.8 to 50.0 and PHYBench 69.8 to 73.8. The 617B model also improves on all nine shared benchmarks, including GPQA Diamond 89.1 to 91.2, HLE 33.6 to 35.4, and FrontierMath 49.0 to 51.0. An important experimental choice is that these comparisons use the same early SFT-only post-training recipe, without RL. That makes the comparison cleaner and supports the claim that the gains come from continued pretraining with Hidden Decoding rather than from downstream alignment differences.

For scaling with expansion factor, the paper runs a progressive study on the 80B model, increasing n from 2 to 4 to 8. MMLU improves monotonically from 85.0 to 86.7 to 87.5, while Pile-test BPB drops from 0.386 to 0.378. The BPB result matters: it shows that Hidden Decoding improves the underlying language-modeling objective, not only reasoning benchmarks after post-training.

The full paper likely includes ablations on persistent KV, stream-specific embeddings, the density of cross-stream exchange layers, and the efficiency trade-off of Stream-Factorized Attention versus denser alternatives. Those ablations are important because they test whether the gains come from the intended mechanism rather than from simply making the sequence longer.1e:T6a9,This one deserves a careful read. Read it in four passes: motivation, systems constraint, method, evidence.

Start with the introduction and focus on why the paper rejects depth looping in favor of sequence-length scaling. The key is not abstract modeling preference but compatibility with pipeline parallelism. Then study the main Hidden Decoding diagram until three pieces are clear: token expansion into streams, loss applied only on the final stream, and persistence of intermediate KV states across positions. After that, read the Stream-Factorized Attention section closely. This is the engineering hinge of the paper. Without it, the method would likely fail at 100B+ scale. Use the complexity discussion and the architecture figure together to understand which layers are intra-stream only and which layers perform cross-stream mixing.

In experiments, prioritize three things. First, the main 80B and 617B result tables: check whether gains are broad and whether they concentrate on reasoning-heavy tasks. Second, the progressive-expansion study: verify monotonicity and inspect diminishing returns as n grows. Third, the ablations, especially the necessity of persistent KV and stream-specific embeddings. If time allows, also read the throughput, memory, and context-length cost analysis, because practicality is part of the contribution.

The deeper questions worth following up are: whether different streams specialize into distinct functions; how training-time expansion should be handled at inference time; how this scaling axis interacts with MoE, long context, and decoding efficiency; and how Hidden Decoding relates to latent reasoning, visible chain-of-thought, and test-time scaling.1f:T45a,The first contribution is notational unification. All architectures are written as recurrent updates over a fixed-size memory matrix W_t, with explicit separation of the delta-rule residual r, decay, erase, and write control, and with scalar versus channelwise gating made explicit. The second contribution is a trainable Megatron-based implementation used to compare these variants at matched scale, mainly 350M-parameter models trained on 15B tokens. The comparison covers optimizer and learning-rate sensitivity, pure versus hybrid stacks, runtime across sequence lengths, downstream behavior, and larger DeltaNet runs at 1.3B and 3B parameters. The third contribution is cross-layer routing. The paper first tests Cross-Layer Error Residuals (CLER), which forward a lower layer’s delta write error to adjust the next layer’s value target, finding no improvement. It then proposes Cross-Layer Value Routing (CLVR), which routes the aligned write value from a lower layer directly into the hidden stream of the next layer, preserving linear-time structure while producing a small validation-loss improvement.20:T411,HALO attaches a lightweight trainable refinement module to the hidden states and logits of a frozen LM. The first component is a coarse refinement path, but in the best reported configuration tokens are not forced to take an initial update. A small controller builds cheap gate features from current logits and, when available, the change in logits from the previous step. It then predicts a keep probability; stable or low-value tokens can skip refinement early. The second component scores eligible tokens and applies monotonic token halting. The reported winning setup uses a learned-gain score, a budget fraction of 0.35, and a minimum of 8 selected tokens. Dropped tokens are not reactivated within the same forward pass. Selected tokens are updated together with a latent scratchpad state, which gives the refinement block a small auxiliary workspace rather than a plain residual update. The paper also emphasizes train-test consistency: the same budgeted routing rule is used when the second-stage path is invoked in fixed evaluation.21:T84c,方法上，论文从一个很朴素但很有力的恒等式出发：沿着从 clean data 到 pure noise 的退化路径，条件熵 H(X|Y(τ)) 的增量望远镜求和后，得到总熵或更一般的 cross-entropy 的守恒关系。关键难点不在积分形式本身，而在于如何把 joint conditional entropy / CE 的导数，化成可训练、可解释的局部量。作者借用编码理论里的 EXIT / GEXIT 思路，证明在 memoryless channel 下，整体导数可以拆成各坐标的局部导数之和。进一步，在 mismatched setting 中，他们把真实数据分布 P 与模型后验 Q_θ 之间的数据-模型 cross-entropy 写成沿噪声参数 τ 的积分，积分核是局部信息导数项。这样一来，diffusion 的全局 CE 被精确连接到每个噪声级别上的局部去噪质量。

更具体地说，论文的几个技术点值得单独看。其一，统一性来自对“admissible memoryless channel”的抽象，而不是只对 Gaussian 或 masking 特判。Gaussian 情况退化到熟悉的 I-MMSE；离散情况则得到对应的 generalized EXIT 公式。其二，作者证明了 locality property：计算这些信息论导数时，不需要完整的联合后验 P(X|Y(τ))，只需边缘后验 P(X_i|Y(τ))，或者进一步写成 P(X_i|Y_{-i}(τ)) 再结合 channel tilt。这个结论很重要，因为完整联合后验在高维序列上几乎不可建模，而边缘后验更接近实际 diffusion LM 的 token-wise 参数化。其三，论文给出一个实现层面的推论：训练时可以只建模 P(X_i|Y_{-i}(τ))，再用已知 channel likelihood 做倾斜修正得到目标后验。这和 masked LM / pseudo-likelihood / leave-one-out 风格目标有明显亲缘关系，但这里给出了更一般的噪声路径版本。其四，作者反复强调 matched 与 mismatched 的分界：在无限容量、精确后验时，不同 channel 的积分都守恒到同一个 CE；但有限容量下，不同 channel 对后验族的逼近难度不同，因此会出现 channel-dependent gap。也就是说，理论上等价，不代表有限模型下训练等价。22:T767,The technical starting point is a telescoping identity over the degradation path from clean data to pure noise. Conditional entropy, and more generally data-model cross-entropy, can be expressed as the integral of its derivative with respect to the noise parameter. The nontrivial step is to turn the derivative of a joint quantity into something local and usable. The paper imports the EXIT/GEXIT machinery from coding theory and proves that for memoryless channels, the derivative decomposes into a sum of coordinate-wise local derivatives.

The main result is a mismatched conservation law for cross-entropy. Instead of assuming the denoiser equals the true posterior, the analysis allows a learned posterior family and shows that the global data-model CE is exactly the integral of local information derivatives along the noise axis. This yields several concrete consequences. One, the framework is channel-agnostic at the level of admissible memoryless corruption and recovers familiar special cases such as the Gaussian I-MMSE relation. Two, there is a locality property: the relevant derivatives depend only on marginal posteriors P(X_i | Y(τ)), not on the full joint posterior P(X | Y(τ)). This is a major simplification for high-dimensional sequence modeling. Three, the paper derives an implementation-oriented implication: it is sufficient to model an extrinsic posterior of the form P(X_i | Y_{-i}(τ)) and combine it with the known channel likelihood through a tilt. That connects the theory to practical token-wise denoisers and to leave-one-out style parameterizations. Four, the paper makes a sharp distinction between matched and mismatched regimes. In the matched limit, all admissible channels conserve the same CE. In finite-capacity settings, however, different channels define posterior families of different complexity, which leads to channel-dependent performance gaps.23:T68e,The experiments are designed to validate the finite-capacity claim rather than to optimize benchmark rankings.

The first set uses synthetic Markov sources with known entropy rates. This setting allows direct comparison between the theoretically conserved quantity and what finite denoisers recover under different channels. By varying alphabet size, the paper shows that channel-dependent gaps grow when the posterior family becomes harder to approximate. This is the cleanest empirical support for the main thesis.

The second set studies character-level language modeling on text8. The key comparison is between discrete noising paths and Gaussian noising paths under comparable model capacity. The paper reports substantial channel-dependent differences in CE/NLL, indicating that some channels align better with the discrete structure of text and are easier for finite denoisers to learn. The most useful plots here are the decompositions over noise levels, which show where the model pays the CE cost along the path.

The third set uses CIFAR-10 to show that the same phenomenon is not specific to text. High-dimensional image data also exhibits large finite-capacity, channel-dependent gaps. The practical message is that the conservation law is universal, but the approximation burden imposed on a given model family is channel-specific.

The abstract already states the main empirical takeaway: synthetic data, text8, and CIFAR-10 all show large finite-capacity, channel-dependent gaps. When reading the full paper, the most important numbers are not a single headline metric but the CE, NLL, or bits-per-dim comparisons across channels, alphabet sizes, and capacities.24:T4ea,Read it in three passes. First, go through the introduction and the main theorem statements. The key points to lock in are: the conserved quantity is data-model cross-entropy, not just entropy; the scope is general memoryless noising processes; and channel choice matters in practice because of finite-capacity mismatch.

Second, study the derivation that turns the derivative of joint conditional entropy or CE into coordinate-wise local terms. Pay attention to the assumptions behind differentiability, absolute continuity, and the memoryless factorization. These details determine how far the result can be extended to practical diffusion LM variants. If your interest is discrete diffusion or masked LM, the most important part is the proof that marginal posteriors are sufficient.

Third, focus on the implementation implication: how P(X_i | Y(τ)) is related to an extrinsic posterior P(X_i | Y_{-i}(τ)) plus a channel-dependent tilt. This is the bridge from theory to trainable denoisers.

CIFAR-10 mainly serves as a universality check. A careful read will likely take 1.5 to 2.5 hours.25:T736,The method is deliberately minimal. Instead of changing attention or introducing a new positional network, the paper keeps the RoPE mechanism and replaces fixed band frequencies with learnable scalars. In the reported setup this adds only 32 parameters per model, which suggests the learned frequencies are shared at the band level rather than expanded per layer and per head. The key point is that the relative-position property of RoPE is preserved: the rotated query-key inner product still depends only on relative offset, but the spectrum is no longer forced to follow a predetermined geometric schedule.

What makes the approach interesting is not just added flexibility, but selective relaxation of the right inductive bias. Compared with learned absolute embeddings, LeRoPE remains a relative positional encoding and therefore keeps the structural advantages of RoPE. Compared with partial RoPE, it does not require manually deciding which low-frequency bands should stop rotating. Compared with changing the base, it does not apply a uniform rescaling to the whole spectrum; it allows non-uniform redistribution across bands. The analysis shows that the learned spectra are highly consistent across scales and random seeds, which argues against the improvement being a fragile optimization artifact.

A second technical contribution is the analysis of attention logits by frequency band. Rather than stopping at perplexity, the paper decomposes positional contributions across bands and finds the emergence of a dominant positional band. This suggests that trained models do not use the RoPE spectrum uniformly. Instead, they seem to concentrate explicit positional signaling in a small part of the spectrum while leaving other bands closer to content channels. LeRoPE appears to help the model discover this allocation more efficiently.26:T652,The experimental setup is a scale ladder from 52M to 2.5B parameters, all trained from scratch. The main empirical result is simple and strong: LeRoPE outperforms standard RoPE at every scale. The clearest quantitative statement in the abstract is that at 2.5B scale, standard RoPE requires 3.4% more compute to match LeRoPE. That framing is more informative than a single validation-loss delta because it directly translates into pretraining efficiency.

The analysis results are equally important. Learned frequency profiles are highly consistent across random seeds and model sizes, which indicates that the optimization is finding a stable preferred spectrum rather than exploiting arbitrary extra degrees of freedom. The paper also shows that one band emerges with a much larger positional contribution to the attention logits than the others, termed the dominant positional band. This supports the view that the useful role of the RoPE spectrum is not evenly distributed.

If you are considering adoption, spend extra time on the appendix for initialization, constraints on the learned frequencies, optimizer treatment, and convergence patterns across scales.28:T8d7,方法建立在 AttnRes 框架上。标准 decoder-only Transformer 有 2L 个 residual-writing sublayers，每个 attention 子层和 FFN 子层都会写一次输出 o_i。普通 PreNorm Transformer 在每个 residual read site 只是把历史写入固定相加；AttnRes 则在 read site t 用一个学习到的 pseudo-query q_t，对历史 source set S_t 做 attention，得到当前 hidden state。原始 AttnRes 直接把归一化后的 o_i 当 key，把 o_i 本身当 value。

论文提出 LR-AttnRes，保留 full-dimensional value path，只把 key 压到 r 维。具体有两个变体。

1. P-LR-AttnRes：Projected Low-Rank Attention Residuals。做法是把原本输出投影从 d 扩成 d+r，一次线性投影同时产出 full residual value 和一个 learned low-rank routing key。这样路由表示由单独参数学习，不再强迫 residual content 自己兼任 key。这个版本的优点是解耦最彻底，表达能力也最强；代价是仍然引入额外投影参数和一部分 FLOPs。

2. S-LR-AttnRes：Sliced Low-Rank Attention Residuals。它不额外学 key projection，而是直接取 full value 的最后 r 个维度作为 routing key。这样做牺牲了一部分解耦程度，因为 key 仍然嵌在 value 里，但省掉了额外参数路径，低秩 routing 带来的 kernel 降本会转化成真实总 FLOPs 降低。这个设计很朴素，但论文结果显示它几乎不损失效果。

论文同时沿用了 Full AttnRes 和 Block AttnRes 两种 source 管理方式。Full 版本对所有历史子层输出做 depth attention，灵活但存储和通信重。Block 版本把连续子层输出按块求和形成 block summary，只保留 embedding、已完成 block 的 summary，以及当前 unfinished partial block。低秩 key 机制可以直接套在这两种版本上。作者的主要结果集中在 Block 版本，因为它更接近可实现的折中点。

从机制上看，这篇工作的关键不是简单“降维”，而是明确区分：residual value 需要高容量，routing key 只需要足够区分深度来源。这个假设如果成立，就意味着 depth routing 的最优表示维度应显著小于 hidden size。论文的实验基本支持这一点，尤其是 r=32 或 64 已经足够。29:T7c0,The method starts from AttnRes in a decoder-only Transformer. Instead of forming the hidden state at each residual read site by summing all previous writes, AttnRes uses a learned pseudo-query q_t to attend over a source set of earlier sublayer outputs. In the original formulation, each output o_i serves as both the value mixed into the residual stream and, after normalization, the key used for depth routing.

LR-AttnRes keeps the value path unchanged but compresses the key path to rank r, with r much smaller than d.

The paper introduces two variants.

1. P-LR-AttnRes. The output projection is expanded from d to d+r, producing both a full residual value and a learned low-rank routing key. This explicitly decouples routing from residual content. It is the more expressive design, since the model can learn a dedicated routing representation.

2. S-LR-AttnRes. Instead of adding a separate key projection, it simply uses the last r dimensions of the full residual value as the routing key. This is less expressive because routing still reuses part of the value representation, but it removes the auxiliary projection path entirely. As a result, the low-rank routing reduction translates into a real reduction in total added FLOPs, not just a cheaper attention kernel.

The paper evaluates these ideas under both Full AttnRes and Block AttnRes. Full AttnRes attends to all previous residual-writing sources. Block AttnRes reduces storage and communication by grouping contiguous sublayer outputs into block summaries, attending only to the embedding, completed block summaries, and the current partial block. The main results focus on the block setting, which is the more practical tradeoff.

The key idea is not just dimensionality reduction. It is the claim that residual values need full capacity, while routing keys only need enough information to distinguish among depth sources. The experiments support that claim: small routing ranks such as 32 or 64 already work well.2a:T593,The headline result is that low-rank routing improves both loss and efficiency. The best validation loss reported is 2.9477 from Block P-LR-AttnRes with 8 blocks and r=32. A nearly identical result comes from Block S-LR-AttnRes with 8 blocks and r=64, reaching 2.9480.

The relative comparisons are more informative than the absolute numbers. The sliced variant improves validation loss by 0.0193 over the strongest standard AttnRes baseline in the same setting, while using 3.25x less added compute. Compared with the best projected model, it is only 0.0003 worse in validation loss but uses 11.3x less added compute. That is the central empirical message: most of the gain comes from low-rank routing itself, while the extra flexibility of a learned key projection adds only a very small margin in this setup.

The paper also reports that the best sliced configuration adds only 0.093% FLOPs relative to the non-embedding Transformer core. That number matters because it shows the method is not just better in principle but close to negligible in overhead.

The experimental scope is still limited. The evidence is centered on validation loss and compute overhead, not large-scale pretraining, downstream transfer, or long-run optimization stability. So the paper supports the claim that low-rank depth routing is a better AttnRes design, but not yet that it should replace standard residual streams in production-scale LLMs.2b:T425,For a quick read, focus on three parts.

First, read the introduction carefully for the argument about representational tension. The paper only makes sense if you buy the idea that using the same tensor as both value and key is a real bottleneck rather than a cosmetic inefficiency.

That makes the routing mechanism closer to a learned depth-specific read head than to fully input-conditioned attention, which has implications for scalability.2c:T61e,The model starts from diagonal SSMs and adds explicit delayed-state feedback. In a standard discrete SSM, the next state depends on the current state and the current input. In DSSMs, one or more delayed states, such as h_{t-τ}, are also injected into the recurrence. This gives the model a direct pathway to preserve and reuse historical information instead of relying entirely on exponentially decaying modes in the current hidden state. The paper has to solve three technical issues. First is stability: delayed feedback makes the system more delicate than standard ODE dynamics, so the authors introduce a practical parameterization and discretization that keep the recurrence stable. Second is history management: a DDE-inspired discrete model needs explicit buffers for past states and careful handling of delay indexing and initialization. Third is parallel training: standard LTI SSMs can be trained via convolution kernels and FFT, but delayed feedback changes the transfer function and creates aliasing and numerical issues in the frequency domain. The paper derives the exact transfer function for the delayed recurrence and proposes a kernel contour shift technique to suppress time-domain aliasing, preserving efficient FFT-based training. The use of diagonal parameterization is deliberate, since it keeps modes decoupled and makes both stability analysis and FFT implementation tractable. Unlike H3 or hybrid attention-SSM models, DSSMs do not add an external recall module; they modify the underlying dynamics to include explicit historical feedback.2d:T477,The experiments are organized around three settings: targeted delayed-memory tasks, efficiency benchmarks, and standard sequence-modeling datasets. The paper is more convincing as a mechanism-validation study than as a large-scale language-model benchmark. On targeted memory tasks, DSSMs outperform standard diagonal SSMs on patterns that require delayed access and precise recall, which is the most important evidence because it directly matches the motivation. On efficiency, the model still supports FFT-style parallel training and linear recurrent inference, showing that delayed feedback does not collapse back into expensive attention. On standard datasets, the delayed-memory mechanism appears to transfer beyond synthetic tasks into broader sequence modeling. For foundation-model readers, the experiments mainly show that the architecture addresses a real weakness of SSMs, not that it already beats mainstream LLM backbones at scale. If you are looking for detailed LM-style reporting with parameter counts, token budgets, and perplexity tables, this paper is lighter there; its emphasis is feasibility and dynamical interpretation.2e:T417,UMoE has three stages. First, it prunes low-saliency experts using target-domain calibration data. The default score is REAP saliency, which combines the magnitude of an expert’s MLP output with its normalized router gate, averaged only over tokens where that expert is selected by top-K routing; unselected experts receive zero score. The method keeps the top half of experts per layer. This is different from routing-frequency pruning, because frequent routing does not necessarily imply strong contribution to the target-domain computation. Second, it regrows the expert pool through perturbation-based expansion from the retained experts, restoring the original number of experts. Third, it applies standard domain SFT. The final model keeps the same number of experts E, active experts K, parameter count, and inference cost. Compared with direct SFT, it explicitly reallocates expert slots; compared with permanent pruning, it preserves capacity; compared with generic upcycling, its expansion source is selected by target-domain saliency.2f:T785,The paper introduces two variants. The base version is a Dirichlet-process cache. For each incoming representation, the model compares it to existing memory-slot keys. If the nearest slot is farther than a threshold, it allocates a new slot; otherwise it merges the input into the nearest slot and updates the corresponding key/value. This is the DP-means rule, the small-variance MAP limit of a Dirichlet-process mixture, but used here as an online write operator rather than latent-variable inference. Readout remains content-based, so the model retains some of the retrieval behavior of attention while avoiding per-token storage.

The second variant is a surprise-adaptive Dirichlet-process cache. A fixed concentration works for stationary streams, but not when novelty arrives in bursts. The paper therefore adapts the concentration using a surprise signal derived from recent allocation rate. When novelty rises, the cache becomes more willing to open new slots; when the stream becomes predictable again, the effective budget tightens and memory consolidates. The two variants share the same allocate-on-novelty and read mechanism. They differ only in whether concentration is fixed or dynamically scheduled.

The distinctions from prior work are carefully drawn. This is not clustered or routing attention, which approximates full softmax within a bounded context and usually uses a fixed number of clusters. It is not Memorizing Transformer, kNN-LM, or other external-memory systems that still store token-level entries. It is also not fixed-budget sparse caching such as StreamingLLM or H2O, where capacity is controlled by eviction. The closest family is novelty-gated memory such as Titans or EM-LLM, but here novelty is defined by a DP-means-style distance threshold rather than a purely learned write gate. The novelty is therefore in the synthesis and in where it sits on the SSM-to-attention design spectrum.30:T575,From the available full text, the experimental agenda is clearly controlled rather than large-scale language-model pretraining. The text repeatedly scopes claims to a controlled setting, which suggests synthetic sequence tasks, copy or retrieval tasks, and diagnostics similar in spirit to Zoology-style recall-throughput evaluation rather than full frontier-scale LM training.

That state space may come from BPE or subword tokenizers, bytes or characters, VQ image tokens, codec audio tokens, video tokens, or natural scientific alphabets such as amino acids, nucleotides, atom types, and bond types. Within this lens, several families become different choices in the same design space. Transition-matrix methods, as in D3PM-style models, specify categorical transitions directly and can support uniform, nearest-neighbor, or structure-aware corruption. Masking or absorbing-state methods introduce a mask token as an absorbing state and train the model to recover clean tokens from partially corrupted sequences; they are related to masked language modeling, but generation proceeds through iterative denoising rather than one-shot filling. Score- or ratio-based methods learn discrete probability ratios or denoising directions rather than continuous scores, covering recent diffusion and flow-matching language models such as SEDD, MDLM, and LLaDA-like systems. The framework also explains why embed-then-diffuse is fragile: adding Gaussian noise in embedding space and rounding back to tokens creates a mismatch between continuous geometry and discrete vocabulary structure. Its evidence is comparative and organizational, spanning diffusion language models for text and code, tokenized multimodal generation, and scientific sequences or structured alphabets. Several practical lessons are emphasized. Token granularity changes the denoising problem: subword tokenization shortens sequences but makes each token semantically larger, while byte or character tokenization increases length but regularizes the alphabet. Vocabulary topology matters: in image or audio codebooks, uniform corruption can destroy local structure that a topology-aware transition matrix could preserve. Absorbing-mask models are convenient for infilling and arbitrary-order generation, but they require careful sampling schedules, confidence-based remasking, or step allocation to reduce train-sample mismatch. Parallel generation is not automatically faster in wall-clock terms; the number of denoising steps, denoiser size, resampling policy, and hardware efficiency determine the realized latency.38:T643,The technical core is to make the extra amplification from repeated visits to shared layers explicit in a first-order perturbation analysis. The starting point is DeepNorm: in Post-LN Transformers, one chooses a skip scale alpha and a residual-branch initialization gain beta so that the cumulative effect of parameter updates on the forward signal stays bounded. For untied depth, the condition is roughly M(beta/alpha)^2 = O(1), where M = 2N counts residual sublayer applications. In a looped Transformer, however, the same physical sublayer is visited R times, so both gradient writing and parameter reading are shared across rounds. The authors introduce a visit-alignment coefficient kappa_R to measure how strongly gradients and sensitivities align across visits. If visits decorrelate, kappa_R stays small and the analysis reduces to the DeepNorm case up to constants. If visits are coherent, kappa_R grows with R, and the shared update is effectively amplified. This yields a loop-aware stability condition kappa_R M(beta/alpha)^2 = O(1). Under the scaling family alpha = (cN)^p and beta = (dN)^(-p), the usual DeepNorm threshold p = 1/4 is recovered in the decorrelated regime, but in the conservative aligned regime with fixed physical depth K and growing loop count R, the threshold shifts to p = 1/2. Based on this, the paper proposes DeepLoop: keep the DeepNorm Post-LN architecture, but use the more conservative scaling alpha = (2N)^(1/2) and beta = (8N)^(-1/2). No gates, auxiliary losses, or learned residual coefficients are added; it is a one-line scaling rule tailored to tied depth.39:T521,1. Adopt the Kronecker-factored Hessian (K-FAC) approximation to decompose per-layer weight Hessian into the Kronecker product of input activation covariance H_X and output gradient covariance H_G, integrating the previously omitted H_G into the quantization objective. 2. Introduce bidirectional incoherence processing applied to both input and output sides. 第一件，是把 prefill attention 重写成适合 XDNA AIE 阵列的三阶段数据流流水线。论文沿用 FlashAttention 的在线 softmax 思路，不显式物化完整 attention matrix，而是按 tile 逐块计算 QK^T、维护每行的 running max 与归一化项，再与 V 累积得到输出。不同点在于，作者不是把它当作单 kernel，而是拆成可分布到多个 AIE tile 的 producer-consumer pipeline。按文中描述，这个 pipeline 将矩阵乘、归一化统计更新、以及后续与 V 的累积等步骤分散到不同阶段，并通过显式数据布局和片上缓冲传递中间量，尽量避免回写外存。

第二件，是数据布局与工作切分的联合设计。XDNA 这类 NPU 的关键不是线程块，而是 tile 上本地存储和 tile 间流式通信。作者针对 Q/K/V 的 tile 化、转置/重排、以及中间统计量的存放做了专门布局，使得每一级都能以较规则的块访问推进。这里的重点不是数学新意，而是把 FlashAttention 中“在线归一化必须跨 tile 保持数值正确”这件事，转成硬件上可流水执行的状态传递问题。论文还强调了与 layer-by-layer 实现的区别：后者把 attention 拆成多个独立算子，频繁落地中间结果；STEEL 则把这些步骤融合成一个持续流动的数据通路。

第三件，也是论文最有信息量的点，是 sparsity-aware pipeline placement。因果掩码使得不同 query block 对应的有效 key block 数量不同，靠近序列开头的块工作量小，靠近结尾的块工作量大。如果按均匀方式把 block 分给流水线阶段或 tile，会出现后段拥塞、前段空转和同步等待。作者利用这种由 causal mask 诱导出的三角形稀疏结构，重新安排 block 在 pipeline 中的位置和分配，使各阶段负载更接近均衡。文中给出的结果是，相比 uniform placement，这一策略单独带来 38% latency reduction。这个点值得注意，因为它不是传统意义上的 sparse attention，而是“对已知结构性空区的执行级利用”。

此外，论文还强调可移植性：同一套数据流 formulation 可以迁移到多代 XDNA-like 架构，并在 XDNA 1 上超过此前 DATO 的实现。这里的可移植不是源码无改动，而是算法分解与流水线组织方式具有架构族层面的复用性。3b:T83f,STEEL has three main components.

First, it reformulates prefill attention as a three-stage dataflow pipeline over XDNA AI Engine tiles. The algorithm keeps the core FlashAttention idea: compute attention block by block, maintain online softmax statistics instead of materializing the full score matrix, and accumulate the output incrementally. The novelty is in how this is decomposed for a spatial NPU. Rather than treating attention as one monolithic kernel, the computation is split into pipeline stages that can run on different tiles with explicit producer-consumer communication through on-chip buffers.

Second, the implementation jointly designs tiling and data layout. On XDNA-like hardware, the critical resource is not just arithmetic throughput but how Q, K, V tiles and intermediate statistics move through local memories and streams. The paper restructures the computation so that the running max and normalization terms required by online softmax can be propagated correctly across tiles without repeatedly spilling large intermediates to external memory. This is the key difference from a layer-by-layer implementation, where attention is broken into separate operators and intermediate tensors are materialized between them.

Third, and most interestingly, STEEL introduces sparsity-aware pipeline placement. Because of causal masking, different query blocks interact with different numbers of key blocks. Early query blocks have less valid work; later ones have more. A uniform placement therefore creates severe load imbalance and synchronization stalls. STEEL explicitly accounts for this triangular workload pattern when assigning work to pipeline stages and tiles. The paper reports that this placement strategy alone reduces latency by 38% relative to uniform placement. This is an execution-level use of structured sparsity, not a modeling change.

The paper also argues for portability across multiple XDNA-like generations. The claim is not that the exact code is universally portable, but that the decomposition and pipeline organization are reusable across this architecture family.3c:T512,The most useful results come from three comparisons.

First, on an AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370, STEEL on the XDNA 2 NPU is compared against FlashAttention on 12 Zen5 CPU cores and the RDNA 3.5 GPU. The reported average energy reduction is 9.17x versus CPU and 1.75x versus GPU. That is a meaningful system-level result for long-sequence prefill.

Second, against a layer-by-layer attention implementation on XDNA 2, STEEL achieves an average 22.8x speedup. This large gap indicates that fused dataflow execution matters much more than small kernel-level tuning on this class of hardware.

Third, on XDNA 1, STEEL reduces latency by 9.6x on average relative to the previous DATO FlashAttention implementation. That supports the portability claim and suggests the gain is not limited to one specific chip generation.

The key ablation is the sparsity-aware placement strategy, which gives a 38% latency reduction over uniform placement. This directly validates the paper’s main systems argument: causal-mask-induced imbalance and synchronization overhead are first-order bottlenecks on NPUs.

If your interest is systems or inference optimization, the two details worth digging into are how online-softmax state is propagated across tiles while preserving numerical correctness, and whether the same formulation can be extended to decode, MQA/GQA, or structured sparse attention.3e:T65c,The method is called signed symmetric quantization. Standard symmetric quantization uses a signed alphabet with z = 0 and a positive absmax scale. The authors observe that because the alphabet is inherently skewed by one extra negative value, allowing the scale to take either sign effectively lets that extra endpoint protect either the negative tail or the positive tail. Flipping the sign of the scale does not introduce a zero point, so the deployed format remains symmetric and avoids the offset-handling overhead of asymmetric quantization.

The main contribution is not merely allowing negative scales, but providing a closed-form sign selection rule that is data-free in deployment and metadata-free when scales are already stored as signed real values. Intuitively, the rule aligns the extra representable endpoint with the dominant outlier direction, reducing clipping-driven error. The paper also provides theory: a worst-case l2 error bound, conditional bound-optimality of the proposed sign rule, and an analytical equivalence between a scale-sign flip and a unit zero-point shift on the same signed alphabet. That equivalence is important because it clarifies what the method gains: a restricted form of asymmetric alignment while preserving the symmetric deployment path.

From a systems perspective, the proposal is compelling because many real formats already store scales as signed floating-point values. In that setting, the change is nearly free. The authors also implement corresponding 2-bit and 4-bit formats in a llama.cpp/GGUF-style setup to show that the idea survives contact with real inference code.3f:T657,The evaluation covers model families including Llama3, Qwen3, and Qwen3.5, with metrics spanning WikiText2 perplexity, few-shot accuracy recovery, and actual deployment throughput and memory. The most striking result is on Llama3 8B at 2 bits: WikiText2 perplexity drops from 103.1 under the conventional positive-scale symmetric quantizer to 17.8 with the proposed signed symmetric variant, and few-shot accuracy recovery improves by 7.9 percentage points. That is a large effect for such a small change, and it confirms that endpoint assignment can dominate error in the ultra-low-bit regime.

The comparison to asymmetric quantization is equally important. On an AMD EPYC Turin CPU, the paper reports that a 4-bit symmetric format can use about 9% less memory and achieve around 2.21x higher prefill and 2.03x higher decode throughput than its asymmetric counterpart. The abstract also reports that the proposed signed symmetric method retains a 1.24x prefill advantage, a 1.08x decode advantage, and 14% memory savings over asymmetric quantization while substantially improving over the conventional symmetric baseline. So the goal is not to beat asymmetric quantization on every accuracy metric, but to recover much of its alignment benefit without giving up the symmetric deployment profile.

A useful pattern in the full results is that gains are largest at the lowest bit widths. As precision increases, the benefit shrinks because one-sided clipping is no longer the dominant error source. A natural follow-up question is whether the same idea can be extended to activation quantization, group-wise mixed precision, or quantization-aware training.41:T713,The method is Progressive Tree Drafting (PTD). Instead of representing drafts as several independent linear continuations, PTD organizes them as a prefix-sharing tree. This serves two purposes: shared prefixes are computed once rather than repeatedly, and branching is coordinated so parallel budget is spent on genuinely different semantic paths rather than near-identical continuations.

The method has three main components. First, tree construction. PTD initializes a drafting tree with seed nodes, obtained either stochastically or from context-aware semantic cues. Each node is only allowed to attend to its ancestors, preserving autoregressive causality along every root-to-node path. Positional encoding is assigned according to ancestor-chain length so the tree input remains compatible with a standard Transformer.

Second, progressive evolution. PTD does not expand the full tree in one shot. It grows the tree step by step: after each forward pass, candidate children are proposed, and a stepwise pruning rule removes low-value or highly redundant branches. This design is important. Unconstrained expansion would quickly inflate the tree and verification cost; progressive growth lets the model first establish coarse semantic alternatives and then allocate compute to the most promising paths.

Third, draft extraction and verification. Multiple root-to-leaf paths are extracted as candidate continuations and then verified with a standard speculative-decoding acceptance procedure. Compared with Self-Draft, which obtains multiple branches through input perturbations, PTD explicitly coordinates branch relationships through prefix sharing and pruning. Compared with LADE-style parallel future-token prediction, PTD is closer to constrained semantic search than to Jacobi-style linear refinement.42:T4ca,From the provided full-text content, the main confirmed result is that PTD consistently achieves up to about 2× decoding speedup across several benchmarks, without auxiliary draft models and without extra training. The motivating analysis in the paper shows that in Self-Draft, more than half of decoding steps contain branches with over 80% similarity, which is the empirical basis for the proposed tree formulation.

The experimental story appears to center on three aspects. First, end-to-end speedup against vanilla decoding and prior speculative baselines such as external-draft methods, LADE, and Self-Draft. Second, the relationship between acceptance rate and draft diversity, showing that the tree structure and pruning improve not only compute reuse but also the usefulness of candidates. Third, structural ablations: progressive update vs. one-shot expansion, pruning vs. no pruning, different tree widths/depths, and different seed strategies.
